conflict_topics: presence of alcohol at a shared-home party
storage/location of alcohol (fridge vs external/void deck)
balancing guests' expectations vs a housemate's religious-based discomfort
dialogue_quality_notes: Agents state clear, realistic reasons: religious discomfort (Agent D) and guests' expectations/sunk cost (Agents B/A).
A concrete location-based compromise (void deck) is proposed and accepted, which resolves the primary incompatibility.
Agent D clarifies early that the issue is alcohol at the party overall, not fridge storage, removing a potential misunderstanding.
evaluation.final_reason: The group agreed to serve the alcohol off-site at the void deck rather than inside the flat. Evidence: Agent B proposed: "What if we have the drinks at the void deck? We can set up a table there." Agent D accepted: "Having it at the void deck... yeah, that works for me." Agent A reluctantly conceded: "The void deck? It'll split the party up. But fine, if that's the only way." Agent A agreed to keep the drinks out of the flat (adjusted) and Agent D accepted that drinks would be available elsewhere; no additional exchange or return was requested.
position_change_notes: Agent D: Initially objected to alcohol in the home, apologized for not mentioning earlier, and ultimately accepted the compromise to move drinks to the void deck.
Agent A: Initially defended having the drinks (bought with own money) but conceded to move them off-site reluctantly: "But fine, if that's the only way."
Agent B and Agent C: B emphasized guests' expectations; C offered an interim mitigation (cooler box) and later supported the void-deck solution.

round_scores.evidence: Agent D: "It's the alcohol. I'm Muslim, so I don't drink. I'm not comfortable with having it at our party." (Introduces a substantive objection to alcohol being present at the shared party.)

Agent A: "I know you don't drink. It's for the other guests." vs Agent D: "...this is my home too. I'm just not comfortable with alcohol being served at a party I'm hosting." (Both sides assert incompatible positions about serving alcohol in the shared home.)

Agent B: "I've invited people from work, too. They'll probably be expecting drinks." (supports serving) and Agent C: "What if we get a cooler box for the drinks?" (mitigation suggested). The core disagreement about having alcohol at the party remains unresolved.
Agent D: "...it's not about the fridge. It's about having alcohol at the party at all. In our home." (Reasserts that the objection is to alcohol being served in the shared home.)

Agent D: "Yes, that's it. It's about drinking in our home." vs Agent A: "But this is a home for all of us. We all agreed to have the party together. Why didn't you say this before?" (Positions remain opposed and tension increases.)

Agent D: "I guess I didn't think about it until I saw the drinks. ... I'm sorry." (apology/softening) and Agent A: "Well, I've already bought all this. And I can't return it." (states practical constraint). Substantive incompatibility about alcohol in the flat remains.
Agent B: "What if we have the drinks at the void deck? We can set up a table there." and Agent C: "That could work." (A concrete compromise proposal appears but is not yet accepted by all parties.)

Agent D: "Having it at the void deck... yeah, that works for me." and Agent A: "The void deck? It'll split the party up. But fine, if that's the only way." (Both parties accept the off-site arrangement; the specific incompatibility about alcohol being at the flat is settled.)

substantive_insights: The real conflict was about alcohol being present at the shared home, not merely about storage location.
Practical constraints (Agent A already bought drinks and cannot return them) shape acceptable compromises.
A neutral external location (void deck) can reconcile guests' expectations with a housemate's religious-based comfort concerns.
